1 # Package sync — user requirements 2 3 What package synchronisation does, what it asks the user, and what it will not do. 4 5 ## Navigation 6 7 - [High level requirements](high-level-requirements.md) — project vision and scope 8 - [Package sync conformance criteria](package-sync-conformance-criteria.md) — these requirements as individually checkable obligations 9 - [Package sync job behaviour](../jobs/package-sync.md) — user guide 10 - [ADR-020](../adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md) — the decision record and the reasoning behind it 11 12 This document states the intent. Where it and any other document disagree, this one is right. 13 14 ## What package sync is for 15 16 Work on one machine, sync, resume on the other. That only works if the software is there: a synced home directory on a machine without the applications gives configuration for programs that will not start. 17 18 Package sync replicates *what software is installed*. Application data belongs to folder sync, which must run after it — installing software writes its own stock defaults, and those have to land before the user's synced settings go on top of them. 19 20 It replicates by **convergence, not by copying**. Both machines' package managers are asked what they have, and the difference is what the sync acts on; no package database, store or installed file is copied between machines. What is synced is a decision — install this, remove that — plus the configuration the target's own package manager needs to carry it out. 21 22 Package sync is one job per package manager — apt, snap, flatpak — plus a job for software no package manager can reproduce. Each is enabled separately, reviewed separately, and can fail without stopping the others. Enabling one authorises pc-switcher to install and remove software on the target. 23 24 ## Vocabulary 25 26 **Source** and **target** are per-run roles. The sync is launched on the source; the target is the machine being changed. The next run may swap them. 27 28 **The holding machine** is the machine that has the item being decided about — the source for something it has and the target lacks, the target for something only the target has. 29 30 An **item** is one thing the user can be asked about: a package, a snap, a flatpak application, an apt hold, a flatpak mask, a configuration file. Its identity is stable across runs, so a decision about it can be remembered. 31 32 A **decision** is the user's answer about an item: apply it, skip it this run, or always skip it in future runs. 33 34 **Machine-specific** describes an item marked "always skip". The job that marked it never touches that item again on that machine of its own accord, whichever machine the sync runs from — it is neither sent to the other machine nor changed by it. Where an approved change would touch it anyway, the user is asked first. 35 36 **Derived** describes plumbing that is synced because approved software needs it — the repository a package comes from, its signing key, a pin, a flatpak remote. It is never a question of its own. 37 38 An **origin** is where software actually comes from — a repository or remote URL. Not its name: two remotes can share a name and serve different builds. 39 40 A **snippet** is a shell recipe, written once, for software no package manager can install. 41 42 **Flatpak scope** is the user or system flatpak installation. **Snap revision** and **snap channel** are the exact build and the update track. 43 44 ## The model 45 46 **A sync goes one way, from source to target.** The source's installed state is what will be replicated on the target. 47 48 **Identity includes the origin.** `gh` from GitHub's repository and `gh` from Ubuntu's archive share a name and are different software. A package is installed on the target from the same origin it has on the source. 49 50 **The user is asked about software; the plumbing is derived.** Approving a package also approves the repository it comes from — a repository without its package does nothing, and a package without its repository cannot be installed. 51 52 **Consent precedes every change.** Nothing is written to the target before the user has approved the changes that job proposes. 53 54 Where an answer follows from something already approved, it is not asked again. Where it does not, it is asked. 55 56 Asking about every package separately would interrupt the user constantly, so questions are gathered into reviews, and repeated decisions of one kind are presented as a single list settled in one pass. That is a preference, not a rule: applying an approved change can reveal something the plan could not know, and a further question is then correct. 57 58 Approving a removal takes a gesture distinct from approving an install, and is never the default. 59 60 **A failure lands on the package it concerns**, or on the configuration item itself where no package is involved. Every approved item is attempted and every failure is named. If a pin, repository or key fails to land, the packages that needed it fail with it, rather than being installed from whatever origin the machine would otherwise use. 61 62 ```mermaid 63 flowchart TD 64 A["plan — reads only"] --> B["review — the user decides"] 65 B --> C["apply the approved changes"] 66 C --> D["report, per item"] 67 C -.->|"an applied change reveals
something the plan could not know"| E["a further question"] 68 E -.-> C 69 ``` 70 71 ## What happens during a sync 72 73 In its validation step, pc-switcher checks every enabled job's prerequisites before any of them changes anything — core behaviour, not specific to package sync. apt additionally refuses to start while the target's dpkg lock is held. 74 75 Snap auto-refresh is paused on both machines for the run and restored afterwards. The pause is timed, so it expires by itself if the run dies. 76 77 Each job then plans, reviews, applies and reports. 78 79 **Plan** issues read commands only: what each machine has, filtered by the standing machine-specific marks, and the difference between them. A question that cannot be derived is asked here rather than in the review — [apt's Ubuntu Pro question (see below)](#esm-repositories--ubuntu-pro) is one, because one of its answers ends the job before there is anything to review. 80 81 **Review** presents one group at a time: items of one kind, all doing the same thing, each carrying its own decision and all settled in a single pass. The default choice for each item is the action that does no harm: *apply* for an install, *skip* for anything that removes or overwrites. Three answers are offered, or two where a permanent decision is not meaningful. 82 83 The two machines are named by hostname wherever the user reads them. *Apply*, *skip this run* and *always skip* name the decisions; they are not what the user reads. Each answer is offered as the act itself — *install*, *skip now*, *never install*, or *keep for good* where the item is already on the machine — and carries a sentence of its own naming the machine the act happens to and how long the answer lasts, so a permanent answer says it will not be asked again. The answers to one question read as a set: one grammar for all of them, and the machine named in every sentence or in none. 84 85 The user can abort the whole sync at any question, and aborting is never read as declining one item. 86 87 **Apply** converges one item at a time, in the order the job requires, and announces every write. Nothing unapproved is written, and no write escapes pc-switcher's per-command confirmation — including the decision records, the snippet registry and the snap refresh pause. 88 89 **Report** gives the job's outcome: success, skipped with the reason, or failed naming each failed item. 90 91 The log holds more than the report. It names every item the job presented and the decision each one got, and every change the package manager made on its own behalf — the collateral the review never showed. The package manager's own output is kept verbatim in the debug log. 92 93 A credential embedded in a URL is withheld wherever the user or the log would otherwise see it — in a command, in a package manager's output, in a configuration file shown whole for a decision. A repository can carry its password in its own address, and a log file is readable by anyone with an account on the machine that wrote it. 94 95 A **dry run** plans and reviews exactly as a real run does — the questions are still asked — then changes nothing and records nothing. A **non-interactive run** — one with no terminal to answer at, such as from cron or a script — asks nothing, treats every item as declined, and reports any job with a non-empty review as skipped. 96 97 ## Decisions and their memory: "machine specific" 98 99 **Apply** does the thing. **Skip** declines it for this run only. **Always skip** marks the item as **machine-specific**. The mark is recorded on the **holding machine** — not necessarily the machine the sync was launched from. 100 101 Example: two machines Atlas and Vega, sync launched from Atlas. Vega has `steam`; Atlas does not, so the sync offers to remove it from Vega. Answering "always skip" writes the mark **on Vega**, because Vega holds `steam`. The reverse case: Atlas has `wireshark`, the sync offers to install it on Vega, and "always skip" writes the mark on **Atlas**. 102 103 A machine-specific item is filtered out before the difference is computed, so it never appears in a later review. Because of that, the repository-conflict question below has to disclose it explicitly. 104 105 Marks never sync between machines. Snippets do, because how to install something is knowledge about the software rather than the machine. 106 107 Repositories and pins cannot be marked machine-specific, whether they are being added, changed or deleted; a flatpak remote is never asked about at all, so there is nothing to mark. Where the two machines disagree about where software comes from, that disagreement keeps surfacing every run instead of being silenced once, and the remedy is to align the two machines. apt's own configuration files *can* be marked, because they say how apt behaves rather than where software comes from. 108 109 Report-only findings cannot be marked either — no machine holds a version difference, and a mark would stop the package syncing rather than stop the report. 110 111 ## apt 112 113 apt sync covers the **manually installed** package set — what the user asked for, not what apt pulled in to satisfy it. With it are synced the repositories and pins that decide where those packages come from, apt's own configuration, and apt holds. 114 115 ### Installing 116 117 ```mermaid 118 flowchart TD 119 A["On the source,
absent on the target"] --> B{"Where did the
source get it?"} 120 B -->|"the distribution"| C["Ordinary install"] 121 B -->|"elsewhere"| D{"Does the target already
offer it from that origin?"} 122 D -->|yes| C 123 D -->|no| E{"Can the source's origin
be replicated?"} 124 E -->|yes| F["Install, naming the origin.
Its repository, key and pin
are synced as a consequence"] 125 E -->|no| G["Report it, with origin
and reason. Do not install"] 126 F --> H{"After the configuration lands,
what would apt really install?"} 127 H -->|"the source's origin"| I["Install"] 128 H -->|otherwise| J["Refuse this one install,
naming both origins.
Continue the run"] 129 ``` 130 131 The review names the origin whenever an install would come from anything other than the distribution. 132 133 The last step is a real check against the target's own state after the configuration has landed, not a prediction. An install that would come from the wrong origin fails alone, naming both, and the run continues. 134 135 Two machines on different Ubuntu mirrors are not two origins: each machine's own distribution source files define what "the distribution" means for it. 136 137 A package from a hand-downloaded `.deb` is not apt-sync's business — see [*Software no manager can reproduce*](#software-no-manager-can-reproduce). 138 139 ### Removing a package 140 141 A package on the target that the source lacks is offered for removal, with "skip" selected as default action. Removal does not purge the package's configuration. 142 143 ### Reporting without acting 144 145 Same package, same origin, same version shows nothing at all. 146 147 Three situations are reported and never acted on: 148 149 - **different versions** — both named; versions float — package managers handle updates, not pc-switcher 150 - **different origins** — both named; takes precedence over a version difference, and is never reported for a mirror difference 151 - **an origin that cannot be replicated** — warning reported with the reason, never installed from somewhere else 152 153 ### Holds 154 155 An apt hold is its own item, decided separately from its package, both when it is added and when it is removed. 156 157 A hold blocks everything: apt will not install, upgrade or remove a held package, not even as an unused dependency. So it serves two intents at once — "never lose this" and "never move this off the version that works" — and apt gives no way to tell them apart. 158 159 That second intent decides how a held package is installed. Everywhere else a version floats, because the user expressed no preference; a hold *is* that preference. So when the source holds a package the target lacks, the target gets the **source's exact version**, not whatever repositories currently offer. If that version is no longer available on the target, the install fails as its own item naming both versions — better than silently freezing the target on a version the user never chose, which nothing would ever move again. 160 161 ### Collateral damage 162 163 Approving an install can make apt remove or downgrade something else, through *conflicts*, *replaces* or version constraints. 164 165 If apt installed that something automatically, the collateral action proceeds silently — apt is resolving its own dependencies. The log names it. 166 167 If it is **manually installed on the target**, the user is asked first about any removal/downgrade/upgrade. The question names the package, says that this machine's apt has it marked manually installed, and says what the approved change would do to it. Three answers, each stating its effect: install anyway, skip and leave the triggering install unapplied, or stop the whole apt sync. 168 169 A package marked **machine-specific** is the case that matters most, and the question mentions explicitly that the package is machine specific. 170 171 A package the user chose to keep is protected too. Only a removal the user *approved* is exempt from this question, and one skipped for this run, or marked machine-specific, keeps its protection. A decision made earlier in this same run counts. 172 173 Declining cancels only the changes that actually cause the collateral. Where several cause it together, all are cancelled and the question says so. It never overwrites a decision the user already gave. 174 175 ### Repositories, keys and pins 176 177 Adding or changing a repository is never a question: it is written because an approved package comes from it, and one that feeds nothing this run syncs is not synced at all. 178 179 Deleting one is a question, but only once nothing on the target still uses it — counted after this run's approved removals, and counting packages marked machine-specific. While anything still uses it, the repository stays and is never raised. The question names the URLs the file declares, not just its filename. 180 181 A repository both machines have with different content is overwritten with the source's version silently — unless the overwrite would repoint a package the target marked machine-specific. Then the user is asked, and shown both versions of the file in full. Declining fails every approved package whose origin depended on that file. 182 183 Only a repository this run writes because an approved package comes from it can raise that question. A differing file nothing approved this run needs, is not written, so there is nothing to consent to. 184 185 The distribution's own source files are written and updated, never removed or offered for removal. Files apt itself does not read are not treated as repository configuration. 186 187 **Signing keys are never a review item.** A key the target lacks is copied byte-for-byte from the source before the repository naming it is written; one that differs is refreshed, unless the target's own distribution packaging owns it. Keys are synced from the source machine, not fetched from the internet. An approved repository deletion may take an unreferenced key with it. 188 189 **Every** pin the source has is written to the target, always, without review: a pin decides which origin wins, and one naming an absent origin does nothing. Deleting a pin only the target has *is* reviewed, and the file is shown whole. 190 191 A pin is never read as a statement about the packages it names. 192 193 apt's own configuration — proxy settings, recommends policy — is reviewed whether it is being added, changed or removed, with the full decision, because no approved package implies whether such a setting should be synced. 194 195 ### ESM repositories — Ubuntu Pro 196 197 If the source carries ESM repositories and the target reports no Ubuntu Pro attachment, the user is asked before anything is written and before any other apt question. Two answers: attach the target now, or skip apt for this run while everything else proceeds. The user is told what to run on the target to attach it. 198 199 Writing them to an unattached target fails invisibly: `apt-get update` succeeds and the failure surfaces later, as a 401 during some unrelated install. pc-switcher cannot attach the target itself. 200 201 "I have attached it" re-probes rather than taking the answer on trust, and may be answered any number of times. Skipping skips the whole apt job, not just the ESM files, leaving apt's configuration untouched. A non-interactive run takes the skip; a dry run warns instead. 202 203 Only whether the target is attached is ever logged or shown. 204 205 ### Applying apt's changes 206 207 All repository-configuration work is applied as one unit: backed up, written in apt's required order, then one refresh of the package lists. If the refresh fails, everything is restored and every approved package that depended on the unit fails by name. If a restore itself fails, the backup is kept and its path named. 208 209 Every derived change is logged as it lands and appears in a dry run's preview. 210 211 ## snap 212 213 snap follows the shape every job has: what the source has is offered for install, what only the target has for removal, what cannot be converged is reported. What is particular to snap: 214 215 ### Revision and channel 216 217 snap converges the source's **exact revision and channel**, where apt and flatpak let versions float: snap keeps per-user data in `~/snap///`, which folder sync can only mirror correctly when both machines are on the same revision. 218 219 So a difference of revision or channel is a change to apply, naming both values, rather than something reported; an install lands the source's revision and channel on the target; and the same revision and channel on both machines produces nothing. 220 221 ### Removing a snap 222 223 Removing a snap leaves snapd's own pre-removal snapshot in place — the only recovery path if the removal was a mistake. 224 225 ### Refresh holds 226 227 Refresh holds replicate as their own items, both when added and when removed. A hold recorded for a snap the source no longer has produces no item. 228 229 ### Sideloaded snaps 230 231 Snaps installed from a local `.snap` file are out of scope (#221). They are ignored on both machines: never installed, never removed, never an item. A run names the ones it found so the user knows they are unmanaged, and does nothing else about them. 232 233 ## flatpak 234 235 flatpak follows the shape every job has: what the source has is offered for install, what only the target has for removal, what cannot be converged is reported. What is particular to flatpak: 236 237 ### Identity 238 239 A flatpak application is identified by its **scope** and its **full reference including branch**. The same application in both scopes, or on two branches, is two independent items — one install and one removal — reported as found. 240 241 Origin is not part of that identity: flatpak refuses to install a reference already present from a different remote, so a difference of origin is reported rather than converged, and takes precedence over a version difference. 242 243 ### Installing an application 244 245 An application is installed from the source's remote or not at all, and that remote is identified by **URL and verification setting, never by name** — checked before the install and read back after it. Either failure fails that one application. 246 247 ### Remotes 248 249 A remote is never a review item, whether it is being added, changed or deleted. It is plumbing, derived from the applications the user approved. 250 251 There is no distribution remote to start from: a remote is synced only because an approved application needs it — including the remote supplying that application's runtime — and is provisioned before the first install. 252 253 **A remote replicates with its trust**, not just its name and URL: its signing key is synced byte-for-byte from the source, a verified remote is never replicated as unverified, and an unverified one is replicated as such with a warning. 254 255 A remote both machines have whose URL or verification differs is repointed silently — unless that would move the origin of a machine-specific application, in which case the user is asked, shown both configurations, and declining fails every approved application that needed the source's URL. 256 257 One the source does not have is deleted once nothing on the target still uses it — after this run's approved removals, counted against what the machine actually has, including applications marked machine-specific. While anything still uses it, it stays. Deleting a remote takes its signing key with it. 258 259 A remote the source restricts with a filter is replicated **with its filter**. The filter is a separate file at a path of the user's choosing — flatpak records the path, not the content — so it is copied byte-for-byte to the same path on the target and re-applied there. Like a signing key, it is derived and never a review item. It is applied after the approved applications from that remote have landed, because a filter can be narrower than what the source has installed and must not block replicating it. If it cannot land, every approved application from that remote fails. 260 261 ### Masks and scopes 262 263 Mask patterns replicate per scope, added and removed alike, whether or not anything currently matches them, and land after the applications. 264 265 A flatpak installation that is neither the user nor the system one is skipped. 266 267 ## Software no manager can reproduce 268 269 Software that arrived on the source by a route nothing can replay automatically. Several kinds, one mechanism: the **install snippet**, a shell recipe written once that is synced with the software. 270 271 - **A hand-downloaded `.deb`** — apt knows the name, but no configured repository offers that version. 272 - **Unowned software under `/usr/local` or `/opt`** — dropped there by an install script or a tarball. The scan is deliberately shallow: it names a finding so the user can decide, it does not walk a tree. 273 - **A sideloaded snap**, and **a flatpak from a local bundle or a dead remote** — out of scope for now (#221). 274 275 Detection runs on the **source** only, so there is no record of what was installed this way on the target and **nothing here is ever removed**. 276 277 Every detected item ends the run with a snippet, marked machine-specific, or skipped for this run. 278 279 A snippet is **opaque** — stored and replayed exactly as written, never parsed. It runs as the target user with no privilege added around it and no standing input, so a command expecting an answer fails rather than hanging the sync. 280 281 Reproducibility is judged by what the **source** holds. The snippet registry is synced; if that would lose or change an entry only the target has, the user is asked and declining aborts the run. A snippet written during a review is replayed in that same run. 282 283 ## When something goes wrong 284 285 Every approved item is attempted, and all failures are reported together, each naming its item. One failed item does not block the rest of its job; one failed job does not stop the others. 286 287 A repository, key, pin or remote has no item of its own to fail on. When one of them fails to land, that failure is charged to every approved package that needed it, and all of those packages fail — including ones that would otherwise have installed, because the origin they were approved for is not there. 288 289 It does not work the other way round. A package that fails to install leaves the repository it came from in place, and leaves the other packages that share it untouched. 290 291 A read that does not answer is different. If a package manager cannot be queried at all, its silence is never read as "this machine has nothing installed", which would propose removing everything on the other machine. It fails once, naming the command, and it fails only its own job — the other jobs still run. An *empty* answer is ordinary data. 292 293 ## What this deliberately does not do 294 295 - **The target's apt configuration is not under line-by-line control.** Repositories, keys and pins appear because a package was approved; declining the package is the only way to decline them. 296 - **A pin cannot be kept on one machine only.** It is asked about every run until source and target have the same pin. 297 - **Version drift and origin divergence are reported, never resolved**, for apt and flatpak. 298 - **Hand-installed software is never removed from the target.** 299 - **A target with no Ubuntu Pro attachment costs the whole apt job for that run.** 300 - **A non-interactive run can answer no review.** There is no file of standing answers and no assume-yes option. 301 - **Machine-specific marks are per job, per machine, and never synced.** 302

1	# Package sync divergences
2	
3	
4	Two seeds from the planning stage were checked and did **not** hold up: dry run does show and answer the review, which is what `PKG-FR-DRY-RUN` asks for; and `--confirm-each-command` does cover the decision records, the snippet registry and the refresh pause, as `PKG-FR-CONFIRM-EACH` requires. Neither is a divergence.
5	
6	## DIV-01 — A failed probe ends the whole run, contradicting the stated failure isolation
7	
8	`PKG-FR-OUTCOME-FAILED` requires that "one failed job MUST NOT stop the others". The orchestrator honours that for `PackageItemFailures` only: that arm records FAILED and continues (`orchestrator.py:1292-1314`). `ProbeFailed` is a plain `RuntimeError` (`probes.py:37`), so it falls through to `except Exception`, which records FAILED and then re-raises (`orchestrator.py:1315-1335`), ending the run.
9	
10	Whether this is wrong depends on which reading is intended. `probes.py:42-48` argues a probe failure means the machine or the tool is broken, which is not a finding about any item and arguably *should* stop everything. `PKG-FR-OUTCOME-FAILED` does not distinguish the two. **Ruling needed:** does a dead package-manager read fail its own job and let the others run, or stop the sync?
11	
12	## DIV-02 — The automation escape hatch writes permanent state and is documented nowhere
13	
14	`PCSWITCHER_PACKAGE_REVIEW_AUTOMATION` takes a JSON `item_id → decision` map and bypasses every prompt, returning `was_interactive=True` (`review.py:580-582`). Because the permanence guards test exactly that flag (`sync_core.py:454`, `manual_installs_sync.py:583`), this path **writes machine-specific marks and install snippets** — the two things `PKG-FR-SKIP-ONCE` and `PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` describe as coming from an explicit human choice.
15	
16	It is deliberately absent from `--help`, the config schema and every doc (`review.py:35-39`), and is intended for integration tests that have no TTY. But an environment variable is not a test-only mechanism: anything that can set it on a real run gets silent, unreviewed, permanent decisions.
17	
18	**Ruling needed:** leave as is and document it as an accepted cost; make the automation path report `was_interactive=False` so nothing permanent is written; or gate it on a test-only signal. Note the second option would change what the integration tests can assert.
19	
20	## DIV-03 — Passwordless-sudo preconditions differ per manager and are stated in no requirement
21	
22	The four jobs have materially different prerequisites, all enforced in `validate()` and none written down outside the code:
23	
24	| | source | target |
25	| - | - | - |
26	| apt | required | required |
27	| snap | required | required |
28	| flatpak | none | only when a system-scope item exists on either machine |
29	| manual | none | none |
30	
31	`apt_sync.py:3876-3891` records why source-side sudo is a hard failure rather than a degradation: without it the `/etc/apt` capture silently returns empty digests and the sync reports success having replicated no repository configuration. `snap_sync.py:701-706` records that the source needs it because the refresh pause writes there, and `snap_sync.py:743-745` that snapd admin-gates even *reading* snap config.
32	
33	This is a user-visible precondition — it decides whether the job can run at all — so it belongs in the requirements. **No conflict, just an omission.** The narrative states it; the articles need an entry.
34	
35	## DIV-04 — Sideloaded snaps: resolved by ruling them out of scope
36	
37	Resolved 2026-07-29. `PKG-NG-SIDELOAD` claimed sideloaded snaps "cannot be reproduced" as an accepted cost, which #221 contradicts — a snippet running `snap install --dangerous` reproduces one. The article is deleted: it described deferred work as a deliberate non-goal.
38	
39	The replacement ruling is that sideloaded snaps are out of scope entirely and ignored on both machines, rather than half-handled. `PKG-FR-SNAP-SIDELOAD` now says so, and the code's remaining half — a sideloaded snap only the target has is still an ordinary removal candidate, so the tool can offer to delete a snap it cannot reinstall — is recorded in the criteria's gap register.
40	
41	## DIV-05 — Cross-manager review is asserted in one comment and denied everywhere else
42	
43	`orchestrator.py:1293-1295` justifies the `PackageItemFailures` arm with "The user approved changes across several package managers in ONE batched review (D-24)". There is no such review. `sync_core.py:8-10` and `review.py:713-715` both state the opposite — batching is per manager, each job reviews its own groups inside its own `execute()`, and there is no coordinator.
44	
45	The behaviour the comment guards is still right (one manager's failures should not cancel another's approved work); only the stated reason is wrong. Code comment fix, no behaviour change.
46	
47	## DIV-06 — The generated decision-file header contains a leaked identifier
48	
49	`state.py:93` writes, into every user's `~/.config/pc-switcher/<manager>.decisions.yaml`:
50	
51	> This file is machine-local and is never synced to any peerfilter_inert. Remove…
52	
53	`peerfilter_inert` is a function name that ran into the sentence. Cosmetic, but it ships to users' machines in a file the requirements describe as the record of their explicit decisions.
54	
55	## DIV-07 — apt and flatpak apply the conflict screen to different candidate sets
56	
57	`PKG-FR-REPO-CONFLICT` and `PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REPOINT` read as one rule in two ecosystems. They are not quite the same rule.
58	
59	apt raises the conflict screen for **every** differing repository file that feeds a machine-specific target package, and approving it forces the write (`apt_sync.py:2267-2285`).
60	
61	flatpak additionally gates on the remote being in the set `_derive_remotes` would provision if the review approved everything — so a remote no approved ref needs is never a question, and answering "overwrite" cannot by itself make a remote travel (`flatpak_sync.py:1420-1429`). The code names this as a deliberate divergence from apt.
62	
63	The reasoning is sound — flatpak has no always-sync bucket to make a remote travel independently — but the articles state the two as symmetric. **Ruling needed:** is the asymmetry intended, and should the articles say so?
64	
65	## DIV-08 — `manual_installs_sync` is not covered by the job-ordering check
66	
67	`PKG-FR-JOB-ORDER` says "the three package-manager jobs" must precede `folder_sync`, and `orchestrator.py:1073` validates exactly those three. Code and article agree.
68	
69	The question is whether the article is right. `manual_installs_sync` also installs software — by replaying a snippet — and that software writes its own stock defaults exactly as an apt package does, which is the whole reason for the ordering rule. The shipped config lists it before `folder_sync` (`default-config.yaml:55`), so the default is correct; nothing catches a user who reorders it.
70	
71	**Ruling needed:** extend the rule to all four, or state explicitly why snippet-installed software does not need it.
72	
73	## DIV-09 — The UAT runbook describes two behaviours that have since been fixed
74	
75	`02-UAT-01-RUNBOOK.md` §4b tells the tester that choosing "Skip" at a collateral prompt "writes `SKIP_ONCE` over EVERY package in the batched removal candidate set, not only the one that produced the collateral … so it also cancels a never-offer-again tick made on `X` in the same review", and instructs them to work around it by splitting the check across two runs.
76	
77	That is no longer true. Attribution narrows the batch by re-rehearsing each candidate alone (`apt_sync.py:2528-2576`), and a skip overrides only `APPLY` decisions, explicitly leaving `SKIP_ALWAYS` intact (`apt_sync.py:2645-2666`). Fixed in `402f7067`.
78	
79	§4d likewise tells the tester to expect the title `Delete repositorys the source no longer has (apt)` and to record the pluralisation as a known cosmetic defect. That was fixed in `ffa06900`; the title now reads `Delete repositories …` (`apt_sync.py:338-341`, `apt_sync.py:2055`).
80	
81	§4a is now stale in a third way: it tells the tester that "leaving one unticked at the review is what makes the never-offer-again screen appear". That screen no longer exists — `9ba0d437` replaced the two-pass checkbox flow with one decision screen per group, where every row carries its own answer and there is no leftover set to re-offer. UAT test 1 in `02-UAT.md` describes the same superseded flow ("questionary checkbox composes with paused Rich Live, installs/removals grouped separately, removals start unticked").
82	
83	A tester following the runbook as written would report three fixes as regressions and would look for a screen that has been deliberately removed. The runbook and `02-UAT.md` both need updating before UAT runs.
84	
85	## DIV-10 — A held package is installed at the wrong version, then frozen there
86	
87	Ruled on 2026-07-29, after the code was written, so this is a known gap rather than a contradiction.
88	
89	An apt hold blocks install, upgrade and removal alike — measured on `ubuntu:24.04`: `apt-get remove` and `apt-get install` on a held package both refuse with `E: Held packages were changed`, and `autoremove` leaves it alone. It therefore carries the intent "do not move this off the version that works" as well as "do not lose this", and apt offers no way to distinguish them.
90	
91	`apt_sync` installs every package by name (`_install_args` → `apt-get install --assume-yes --no-install-recommends <name>`) and applies the hold as a separate item afterwards. So where the source holds a package the target lacks, the target installs whatever version its repositories currently offer and then freezes on it — permanently, since nothing will move a held package again. The two machines end up held at different versions with nothing reporting it.
92	
93	`PKG-FR-APT-HOLD-VERSION` now requires the source's exact version for that case, with failure naming both versions where the target cannot supply it. Recorded in the criteria's gap register.
94	
95	**Still unruled:** the same package held on *both* machines at different versions. `PKG-FR-APT-HELD-TARGET` suppresses any package-level item for a held target package, and a hold present on both sides produces no hold item either, so that divergence is currently invisible in every run. Converging it would mean unhold → install the source's version → re-hold, which is a larger change than the install case.
96	
97	## Ambiguity flagged for the Stage 5 article audit — done 2026-07-30
98	
99	`PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` says the item is "never to be offered again on that machine. The mark MUST be local to that machine" with no antecedent for either "that machine". The rule the code implements is the holder rule (`sync_core.py:213-223`): install and change diffs record on the source, removal diffs on the target, written through that machine's own executor. The article was unstatable without a name for the holding machine, which the narrative's vocabulary section now introduces; the article uses the term and drops its inline gloss.
100	
101	The full audit ran over all 123 articles on 2026-07-30. Ten findings, all in the criteria and all vocabulary rather than substance: `rehearsal` for the narrative's *dry run*; `provenance` for *origin*, which the criteria itself contradicted by saying *origin divergence* elsewhere; `prompts` and `a screen` for what the user is asked; `Skip-once` for the narrative's decision words; `blocks` as a collective noun the narrative never defines; `in either direction` on the banned list; two articles carrying two Why lines that said the same thing twice; and `PKG-FR-ASK-WHEN-NOT-DERIVABLE` claiming to enumerate every non-derivable question while omitting four of them. No article was found that could not be stated in the narrative's vocabulary once reworded.
102	
103	## DIV-11 — A filtered remote is replicated unfiltered
104	
105	Ruled on 2026-07-29, after the code was written, so this is a known gap rather than a contradiction.
106	
107	**Measured** (flatpak 1.14.6, `02-SPEC-snap-flatpak-derivation.md` §2.8): `flatpak remote-modify --filter=/tmp/f.filter <remote>` records the *path* `/tmp/f.filter` in the remote's `filter` column and adds a `filtered` token to `options`. The filter's content is an ordinary file at that arbitrary local path, outside the ostree store.
108	
109	The original reading was that this makes the filter unsyncable — "not repository-or-key material". It does not. The content is a file, and the run already carries files byte-for-byte: a repository's signing key is copied exactly this way. What the earlier decision actually gave up on was the *path*: it is arbitrary, so replicating the filter means the flatpak job writing to a location it does not own, possibly inside `folder_sync`'s territory.
110	
111	`PKG-FR-FLATPAK-FILTER` now requires the filter to be replicated: copied byte-for-byte to the same absolute path on the target, re-applied to the replicated remote, derived rather than reviewed, and applied after the approved applications from that remote have landed. Failure to copy or re-apply fails every approved application from that remote.
112	
113	`flatpak_sync` implements the opposite: `_FLATPAK_REMOTES_CMD_TEMPLATE` requests `name,url,options`, so the path is never read, and the shipped behaviour is one WARNING per filtered remote naming the `remote-modify --filter` command. Implementing the requirement widens the capture to four columns, which reshapes every remote fixture in the suite — with the `filter` column requested, an unfiltered remote prints four fields, not three.
114	
115	`docs/jobs/package-sync.md:252` documents the shipped warning behaviour and stays accurate until the code changes.
116	
117	**Open within this ruling:** the ordering rule is stated as a design requirement, not from measurement. Whether flatpak actually refuses to install a ref its own filter excludes has not been tested.
118	
119	## DIV-12 — A skipped removal loses its collateral protection
120	
121	Found on 2026-07-30 while checking the narrative's collateral claim against the code. This is a shipped bug, not a requirement that moved.
122	
123	`_collect_plan_time_collateral` builds `reviewed_names` from the install and removal candidate lists (`apt_sync.py:2586-2588`), before the review runs and therefore before any answer exists. `_classify_collateral` then skips every package in that set (`apt_sync.py:2670`). The comment justifies it as "a decision the user is taking anyway" — true for a removal the user approved, false for one they skipped.
124	
125	So: a package offered for removal, kept by answering *skip*, is excluded from collateral protection for the rest of the run. Approving an unrelated install whose transaction removes it deletes it with no question and, per `PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-AUTO`'s classification, no review line either. The user asked to keep it and it goes.
126	
127	`PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MANUAL` now states that only an APPROVED removal exempts a package. Recorded in the criteria's gap register.
128	
129	## Rulings that close earlier divergences
130	
131	- **DIV-07** (apt's repository-conflict question is wider than flatpak's) is ruled: both ask only what the approved changes need. `PKG-FR-REPO-CONFLICT` now gates on the repository being one this run writes for an approved package. The code still asks more widely.
132	- **DIV-08** (`manual_installs_sync` outside the job-ordering check) is ruled: the rule covers all four package jobs. `orchestrator.py:1082` validates three.
133	- The ESM cost question behind `PKG-FR-ESM-GATE` is answered by measurement rather than ruling: on an attached Ubuntu 24.04 desktop, 60 of 2297 installed packages resolve their candidate to `esm.ubuntu.com`, including `ffmpeg`, `gimp` and `imagemagick`. The container's zero was an artefact of its package set.
134	
135	## DIV-13 — A repository credential reaches the log
136	
137	Ruled on 2026-07-30, after the code was written.
138	
139	A private PPA or a commercial repository carries its credential in the URL itself (`REDACTED`), so the URL is the secret. `Executor._announce` traces every command verbatim at DEBUG (`executor.py:154`), the repository-conflict question shows both machines' copies of a source file in full, and `PKG-FR-LOG-VERBATIM` now adds the manager's own output. Nothing in the codebase redacts anything — `grep -rn redact src/` finds no match.
140	
141	Logs are written to `~/.local/share/pc-switcher/logs` with mode `rw-rw-r--`, so the exposure is to every account on the machine that wrote the log. It does not spread: pc-switcher's own runtime files are excluded from `folder_sync` ahead of any user filter and cannot be re-included (`default-config.yaml:135-137`).
142	
143	`PKG-FR-CREDENTIAL-PRIVACY` now requires the embedded credential to be withheld wherever a URL is written or shown. Recorded in the criteria's gap register.
144	
145	Related, and already satisfied: `PKG-FR-ESM-PRIVACY` is honoured by construction rather than by filtering — `pro status --format json` is parsed and only the `attached` boolean escapes (`apt_sync.py:113-114`, `278-281`).
146	
147	## DIV-14 — The log records counts, not decisions, and no manager output at all
148	
149	Verified on 2026-07-30 against the current head, after the logging requirements were ruled on.
150	
151	`PKG-FR-LOG-DECISIONS` asks for every item a job presented together with the decision it received. What the code writes is:
152	
153	- one FULL line per item that was actually applied — `f"{diff.action.value} {diff.label}"` (`sync_core.py:493`) — or, in a dry run, one `Would …` line per item (`sync_core.py:397`);
154	- INFO counts around them: how many changes are being applied, how many succeeded, how many failed with a joined summary (`sync_core.py:385-416`);
155	- in a non-interactive run, a WARNING carrying the COUNT of unresolved items (`review.py:822`) and one line per group that was not asked (`review.py:914`).
156	
157	So an item the user skipped produces no line at all, and no line anywhere pairs an item with its decision. Auto-collateral is likewise absent — `_classify_collateral` deliberately produces "nothing, not even a report line the user cannot act on" (`apt_sync.py:2655-2656`), which `PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-AUTO` now overrides.
158	
159	`PKG-FR-LOG-VERBATIM` asks for the manager's own output verbatim in the debug log. `Executor._announce` traces the command TEXT at DEBUG before running it (`executor.py:154`); nothing traces what came back. The only output that reaches the log is `stderr` attached as structured context on error paths (`sync_core.py:489`, `apt_sync.py:3551-3557`). No stdout, at any level.
160	
161	Both are recorded in the criteria's gap register. Note the interaction with `PKG-FR-CREDENTIAL-PRIVACY` (DIV-13): implementing verbatim output without the redaction point puts repository credentials in a world-readable file, so the two land together or not at all.
162	
163	Log volume is a known consequence, not an objection: runs on the maintainer's desktop already produce 350-378 MB logs, and the ruling was "all of it, as written".
164

result.output:
1	"""`apt_sync`: apt package convergence — install, remove, and the full diff taxonomy
2	(D-01, D-03, D-04, D-07, D-24, D-25, ADR-020).
3	
4	Captures the source's `apt-mark showmanual` set with `dpkg-query`-sourced versions
5	(never `apt list --installed` — its own manpage says the output has no stable scripting
6	contract), diffs it against the same query on the target into every D-25 class this
7	manager produces (`diffing.diff_apt_packages`, this job's own — the base class holds no diff
8	for anyone to inherit, D-15), and converges the approved `INSTALL`/`REMOVE` items via
9	`apt-get install`/`apt-get remove`.
10	
11	A package is matched by (name, ORIGIN), never by name alone (ADR-020 D-34). The target
12	having a candidate for a name is not evidence it can supply the source's software: one name
13	is often offered by two vendors, and Ubuntu's `firefox` carries epoch 1, which outranks
14	every unpinned vendor version, so an install matched by name replicates the name and
15	inverts the origin. `plan()` therefore reads where the source installed each package
16	from, maps that back to the repository file on the SOURCE that declares it, and classifies
17	the package against the target's real candidate origins: same origin -> ordinary install;
18	different or absent origin with a writable declaring file -> install, with that repository
19	derived from the package's own approval; no writable declaring file -> `REPO_UNAVAILABLE`,
20	reported rather than installed from somewhere else. A package installed on both machines
21	from two different vendors is `ORIGIN_MISMATCH`, report-only.
22	
23	That classification is not the guarantee — it is only what decides which repository work to
24	derive. The guarantee is `origins.OriginClassifier.refusal` (D-35): after this run's single
25	`apt-get update` and before its first install, ONE batched `apt-cache policy` re-reads the
26	target's candidate origins, and an approved install apt would now satisfy from none of the
27	source's origins fails as its own item (D-27), naming both. It sees the state the derivation
28	actually produced, so a repository whose write failed or a pin that never landed is caught
29	there rather than shipping the wrong vendor's package. Packages the source has only from its
30	own distribution files are exempt: two machines on different Ubuntu mirrors are one vendor.
31	
32	That refusal is for a request that is wrong, which is per-item. A probe that did not run at
33	all is a different thing and gets a different answer: `commands.require_apt_answer` fails the
34	run once, naming the command, rather than blaming N packages' origins for a transient
35	network, an apt lock or an interrupted dpkg.
36	
37	Bare-`.deb` packages are NOT in scope and are dropped at capture
38	(`probe.AptProbe.capture_source_items`). A package whose installed version comes from no
39	configured repository was put there with `dpkg --install`; apt cannot install it on the
40	target, and `manual_installs_sync` offers it as an install snippet in the same run (D-18).
41	Both jobs compute the predicate from the shared `packages/apt_policy.py` parser — the same
42	test, never a result passed between them, since D-15/D-16 keep the four jobs independent.
43	
44	The ownership split has a consequence this job may not paper over: `manual_installs_sync`
45	has its own enable flag, and reading another job's flag is exactly the coupling D-15
46	forbids. So enabling `apt_sync` while disabling `manual_installs_sync` leaves these packages
47	replicated by nobody — silently absent rather than offered as installs that fail. Documented
48	for the user in `docs/jobs/package-sync.md`.
49	
50	Every approved item's transaction is simulated with `apt-get --dry-run` before the real
51	command runs, guarding against apt silently doing more than the review showed. Collateral
52	effects are classified by origin (D-30): a package the simulation would remove or
53	downgrade that is auto-installed (not in the target's `apt-mark showmanual` set) is apt
54	resolving its own dependencies and proceeds silently, while a manually-installed one is
55	something the user chose to have and is refused unless the user approved losing it. `plan()`
56	runs two BATCHED simulations (the whole install candidate set, the whole removal candidate
57	set — not one per-package, which would cost more than the sync itself for 150 packages) and
58	classifies their collateral against the target manual set, emitting a three-way
59	go-ahead / keep-the-package / stop-the-sync review item for each manual-collateral package so
60	the decision is made in the batched review, never as a prompt during apply. A batch that
61	turns up manual collateral then simulates each candidate alone, so `skip` cancels the
62	packages that actually cause the collateral rather than everything the user was reviewing
63	(`collateral.Collateral.for_direction`).
64	
65	One install is admitted to no plan-time simulation at all
66	(`origins.OriginClassifier.target_resolvable`, D-40): a D-34 class-3 package, whose
67	repository this run derives from its own approval and writes during converge. Until that
68	write lands the target's apt has never heard the name and `apt-get --dry-run` refuses the
69	WHOLE batch containing it, which would strip the protection from every other package in the
70	run rather than weaken it for one. The exclusion keys on the target's own `apt-cache policy`,
71	never on the simulation's exit code, which cannot separate "unable to locate" from a held
72	dpkg lock (ADR-022 D-01). What covers those packages instead is the per-item simulation
73	`packages.PackageConverger.install` runs after the repository unit has converged, where apt
74	CAN resolve them: unapproved manual collateral fails that one item, so the user is told
75	afterwards rather than asked beforehand.
76	
77	The same plan-time-classification rule covers the `/etc/apt` removal direction (C26): a
78	source file offered for deletion because the source machine no longer has it carries, in
79	its review `detail`, the machine-specific packages the target still installs from that
80	repository. Those packages are recorded skip-always, so `filter_inert` keeps them out of
81	the target manifest and they produce no diff of their own in any run; without this the
82	review shows a bare file deletion and nothing else. Disclosure, not refusal: removing a
83	repository whose packages are going too is legitimate, so the removal stays offered (and,
84	like every removal group, unticked).
85	
86	Neither is `/etc/apt` itself, in most directions. Only what the user has a basis to judge
87	is an item (ADR-020 D-37): a repository REMOVAL, a pin REMOVAL, and apt config in all
88	three directions. Everything else under `/etc/apt` is derived and written without a
89	question, in three buckets `derived.DerivedWrites` assembles from the accepted decisions:
90	
91	- the repository files serving the packages the user approved (ruling 4 — a repository
92	  that feeds no package this run syncs does not travel at all);
93	- every `/etc/apt/preferences.d` file the source has, always. A pin decides which origin
94	  wins, which is precisely what origin replication turns on, and one naming an origin the
95	  target does not have is inert — so always-sync costs nothing and cannot derive wrongly;
96	- the distribution's own source files — `ubuntu.sources`, the two `ubuntu-esm-*` files and
97	  `/etc/apt/sources.list` — written when missing and overwritten when different, never
98	  removed and never offered for removal (D-38).
99	
100	The two `ubuntu-esm-*` files carry the one question this job asks that is not about an item
101	(`esm_gate.EsmGate`, D-38). Writing them to a target with no Ubuntu Pro attachment is not
102	harmless: `esm.ubuntu.com` serves its INDEX publicly, so the refresh succeeds and the ESM
103	suites win candidate selection, and the failure surfaces much later as a 401 on the `.deb`
104	of the target's next install of an ESM-covered package — a failure nobody traces back to a
105	sync. pc-switcher cannot attach the target itself (`pro attach` needs a subscription token
106	or a browser flow, and a machine's own credentials are root-only and not reusable), so it
107	asks, with exactly two answers: attach now, which RE-PROBES rather than trusting the answer
108	and may be given any number of times, or skip `apt_sync` for this run while every other job
109	runs. A run with nobody to ask takes the skip; a dry run warns instead. Skipping the whole
110	job rather than withholding the two files is the only coherent partial outcome, because
111	`preferences.d` always-syncs with no derivation predicate and the source's ESM pins would
112	land regardless. The gate sits in `plan()`, right after the origin state supplies the
113	digests its trigger reads and before any review group is built: one answer ends the job, so
114	it must precede the planning and the review the user would otherwise answer for nothing.
115	Only the parsed `attached` boolean ever leaves `esm_gate` — the probe's payload names the
116	subscriber's account.
117	
118	A derived write has no item, so it cannot fail as one. It is recorded against its
119	destination and charged to every approved package whose origin depended on it (D-39):
120	the refusal lands on the thing the user actually decided about, naming the file. A rollback
121	marks every derived write failed, exactly as it already does every reviewed group item.
122	
123	A signing key is NOT an item either. It has no `ItemClass`, no `item_id`, no diff, no
124	review entry and no decision-file identity: the user thinks in repositories and packages,
125	and a key is only how a repository is made to work. Keys are two plain file operations
126	bracketing the repository unit (`keyrings.py`):
127	
128	- provisioning runs BEFORE any source file is written. It copies every source
129	  `/etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d` key the target lacks or differs on, and the keyrings named by
130	  the source files this run actually writes (a repository this run overwrites may point at
131	  a keyring the target has never seen). `keyrings.Keyrings.gap` still refuses to write a
132	  source whose keyring did not arrive, so a repository is never written ahead of its key —
133	  and that refusal, like every other derived-write failure, is charged to the package.
134	  Provisioning is ownership-aware in ONE direction: a keyring the target LACKS is copied
135	  whatever owns it on the source, but a keyring the target already has with different bytes
136	  is left alone when the target's own dpkg owns that path — the target's package manages
137	  that file and clobbering a distro keyring is not this job's business. Ownership must not
138	  gate the COPY, because a vendor `.deb` (`code`, `tailscale-archive-keyring`) ships both
139	  its `sources.list.d` entry and its keyring, so the repository the package comes from
140	  cannot be trusted until the key that package owns is already there; skipping
141	  package-owned keys would make that bootstrap unsatisfiable. Every derived write is
142	  logged at FULL as it lands, and previewed under `--dry-run` (ADR-014), which is how a
143	  file with no review entry stays visible without becoming a question.
144	
145	Three key directories are captured, not two: `/etc/apt/keyrings`, `/etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d`
146	and `/usr/share/keyrings`. The last is where `add-apt-repository`, several vendor `.deb`s
147	and Ubuntu itself put keyrings, and most real `Signed-By:` values point there; leaving it
148	out made every such reference resolve to nothing and downgraded the repository to
149	`REPORT_ONLY`. Like `/etc/apt/keyrings` it is provisioned only for keys a source actually
150	references, and unlike it, it is never collected: it is package territory.
151	
152	- collection runs AFTER every source write and deletion, and only when this
153	  run actually removed a source file. It re-scans the target's REAL source files and drops
154	  each `/etc/apt/keyrings` file no surviving source references. Counting against the
155	  post-write state is what makes the hard cases come out right: a repository this run
156	  deleted stops counting as a reference, while one the user left unticked, one recorded
157	  machine-specific, and one pc-switcher never syncs at all (`/etc/apt/sources.list`) all
158	  keep counting.
159	
160	Legacy `/etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d` keys are replicated but never collected: they are ambient
161	trust with no discoverable referent, so "unused" is not computable for them and they are
162	allowed to accumulate rather than be deleted on a guess.
163	
164	Keys travel byte-for-byte and are never re-fetched from a vendor (D-12).
165	
166	This job reviews once per run before its first mutating command (ADR-020 D-24), and asks
167	again only where applying an approved change reveals a fact the plan could not know — the
168	requirements' own model, and a preference rather than a rule. Nothing this run writes can
169	invalidate a decision it already took: a package is classified from the SOURCE's origins,
170	which no run mutates, and the one fact that genuinely depends on the target's post-write
171	state — which origin actually wins — is not guessed at plan time at all, it is read back by
172	`origins.OriginClassifier.refusal` and turned into a per-item refusal rather than a question.
173	
174	That is also why a pin says nothing about the packages it names (D-25). A per-package
175	"pinned" report would fire for every package a target-side `preferences.d` stanza names,
176	turning a no-op into review noise and — worse — making a package present only on the target
177	and named by any pin impossible to REMOVE (a `REPORT_ONLY` echo outranks its own
178	`EXTRA_ON_TARGET` diff) and impossible to silence (a `REPORT_ONLY` item cannot be recorded
179	skip-always). Pins themselves DO replicate, as FILES under `/etc/apt/preferences.d`, and
180	that is the whole mechanism: a report about them was never part of it.
181	
182	## Where things live
183	
184	Reads produce frozen facts (`probe.py`); the deciding half — `origins`, `diffing`,
185	`derived`, `keyrings`, `collateral` — is pure over them; only `etc_apt`, `packages`, `files`
186	and `esm_gate` touch a machine. `items.py` says what an apt item is and where its file
187	lives, `messages.py` holds every sentence the user reads, `commands.py` every apt command
188	this job builds.
189	"""

211	    async def plan(self) -> PackagePlan:
212	        """Read-only. The package diff, extended with plan-time transaction-collateral
213	        classification (D-30) and the `/etc/apt` item classes (D-11/D-12/D-13).
214	
215	        Unreproducible detection is NOT apt's business (D-18): it moved to
216	        `manual_installs_sync` with its own enable flag, so this job never emits an
217	        `UNREPRODUCIBLE` diff.
218	
219	        The origin state is captured FIRST, ahead of the package diff: a package's diff class
220	        depends on which repository file on the source declares its origin (D-34), so the
221	        `/etc/apt` reference scans are an input to the package diff rather than a by-product of
222	        the repository one.
223	
224	        The ESM gate (D-38) runs next, for three reasons that each rule out a later spot:
225	        one of its answers ends the job, so it must precede the expensive planning and a
226	        review the user would otherwise answer for nothing; its probe is a read, and this is
227	        the last read-only phase; and it puts the target's environment problem and its
228	        copy-paste remedy on screen before anything is approved or written. Not `validate()`
229	        — every `ValidationError` is fatal (`orchestrator.py`, `models.py`), so there is no
230	        way to express "the user answered, carry on".
231	
232	        Collateral classification runs AFTER the base diff and BEFORE review groups are
233	        (re)built, so every manual-collateral package becomes its own three-way review item
234	        decided in the SAME review the user approves from — never a prompt during apply.
235	        """
236	        source_facts, target_facts = await self._probe.capture_origin_state()
237	
238	        pending_esm = self._esm.pending(source_facts.source_digests, target_facts.source_digests)
239	        if pending_esm and not await self._esm.allow(pending_esm, context=self.context):
240	            # Dry run only (`EsmGate.allow`): a real run has raised by now. Withholding
241	            # keeps the preview from claiming writes no real run would make.
242	            self._esm.withhold(pending_esm)
243	
244	        origins = OriginClassifier(
245	            machines=self.machines,
246	            source_refs=source_facts.refs,
247	            target_refs=target_facts.refs,
248	            source_keys=source_facts.keys,
249	        )
250	        base_plan = await self._plan_packages(origins)
251	
252	        collateral = Collateral(
253	            target=self.target,
254	            machines=self.machines,
255	            target_manual_set=await self._probe.capture_target_manual_set(),
256	            origins=origins,
257	        )
258	        collateral_diffs = await collateral.plan_time(base_plan.diffs)
259	
260	        repo_diffs = await self._plan_repo_diffs(source_facts, target_facts, origins, collateral)
261	
262	        if not collateral_diffs and not repo_diffs and not self._conflicts:
263	            return base_plan
264	
265	        # Ordering is an apt FACT (key before source before packages, T-02-16), not a
266	        # general one: the base loop stays a plain item-by-item iterator, and THIS job
267	        # sorts its own diffs before they reach it. `sorted` is stable, so within one
268	        # rank (e.g. every APT_PACKAGE diff, or every APT_PIN/APT_CONFIG diff) the
269	        # original relative order — base diff, then collateral, then repo diffs — is
270	        # preserved.
271	        # This job's OWN extra diffs (repo files) also need the D-08a inertness pass the
272	        # package half already ran over its diffs — they are derived from directory digests,
273	        # so no input item carried their id into `filter_inert`. The decision files
274	        # `_plan_packages` just read are reused rather than re-read.
275	        all_diffs = self._drop_inert_diffs(
276	            sorted(
277	                (*base_plan.diffs, *collateral_diffs, *repo_diffs),
278	                key=lambda diff: ITEM_CLASS_ORDER.get(diff.item_class, 3),
279	            ),
280	            *self._plan_decisions,
281	        )
282	        return PackagePlan(manager=self.manager_id, diffs=all_diffs, groups=self._build_review_groups(all_diffs))

284	    async def _plan_packages(self, origins: OriginClassifier) -> PackagePlan:
285	        """The package half: load decision files -> capture -> query -> diff -> build review
286	        groups. Read-only.
287	
288	        Both machines' decision files are loaded first (a read, like everything else here)
289	        and each side's captured/queried items are filtered through its OWN file before
290	        diffing (D-08): an item recorded on the source is dropped from the source
291	        manifest so it is never pushed to a peer again; an item recorded on the target
292	        is dropped from the target query so it is never proposed for
293	        install/remove/change again — either way it produces no `ItemDiff` and never
294	        reaches the review.
295	
296	        The finished diffs go through `_drop_inert_diffs` as well, which catches the
297	        recorded items no input-side filter can see: the `apt:hold:` membership items are
298	        derived from hold-set membership, and the post-diff pass is the only CORRECT place
299	        for them anyway — the target hold set additionally suppresses a held package's own
300	        install/upgrade action, so filtering that input set would re-propose upgrading a
301	        held package. `plan()` runs the same pass again over the repository and collateral
302	        diffs it appends.
303	        """
304	        source_decisions = await DecisionFile(self.manager_id, self.source).load()
305	        target_decisions = await DecisionFile(self.manager_id, self.target).load()

402	    def _build_review_groups(self, diffs: Sequence[ItemDiff]) -> tuple[ReviewGroup, ...]:
403	        """Carve apt's two non-standard screens out of the ordinary checkbox groups.
404	
405	        Repository and pin DELETIONS (ADR-020 D-07) become
406	        `REPO_REMOVAL_REVIEW_ACTION` groups: still checkbox lists, still unticked, but
407	        offered only two answers because a permanent machine-local mark on a file whose
408	        purpose is to feed packages would silently change where those packages come from
409	        forever. Manual-collateral diffs (D-30) become a `COLLATERAL_REVIEW_ACTION` group
410	        whose entries take the three-way go-ahead / keep-the-package / stop-the-sync
411	        resolution.
412	
413	        Both trail the base groups — packages and apt config — so the user sees the bulk of
414	        the diff before being asked to resolve anything, and collateral comes last because
415	        it is the only screen that can abort the run.

417	        The unreproducible carve-out is gone (D-18: that concern moved to
418	        `manual_installs_sync`).

421	        removals = [diff for diff in diffs if is_repo_removal_diff(diff)]
422	        if not collateral and not removals and not self._conflicts:
423	            return super()._build_review_groups(diffs)

426	        rest = [diff for diff in diffs if diff.item_id not in carved_ids]
427	        groups = list(super()._build_review_groups(rest))
428	        if self._conflicts:

431	                    manager=self.manager_id,
432	                    action=REPO_CONFLICT_REVIEW_ACTION,

464	                        )
465	                        for diff in entries

471	                ReviewGroup(

473	                    action=COLLATERAL_REVIEW_ACTION,
474	                    title=(

494	    @override
495	    def accept_review(self, plan: PackagePlan, outcome: ReviewOutcome) -> None:
496	        """Insert the synthetic metadata-refresh diff once the decisions are known, so it
497	        flows through the same per-item logging, dry-run gate and failure collection as
498	        everything else (`apply()`'s existing loop) instead of being a special case bolted
499	        onto the end.
500	
501	        Runs AFTER `plan()` (so decisions exist) and is exactly where D-24's review
502	        already stopped being relevant for THIS item — the refresh is infrastructure
503	        the user never ticks, not a repository they decided about. Positioned immediately
504	        after the last non-package diff (repository group already sorted
505	        pin/config-before-source by `plan()`) and before every package diff, matching
506	        apt's own dependency order: metadata must be current before anything installs
507	        from it.
508	
509	        The marker is ALSO what carries the work no diff represents: the derived writes
510	        (ADR-020 D-37/D-38 — a repository, a pin or a distribution file travels without a
511	        review line, so nothing else would ever route into the repository unit), and a
512	        rotated keyring, which changes no source file at all. `Keyrings.pending_work` is a
513	        superset test — the unit recomputes the exact set from the real decisions and returns
514	        early if it is empty — so the cost of a false positive is one no-op call.
515	
516	        Manual-collateral decisions (D-30) are resolved first: a go-ahead on a
517	        collateral item marks its package approved so the apply-time guard lets the
518	        removal through, while a skip is translated into `SKIP_ONCE` on the approved
519	        packages that cause that collateral, so a declined collateral cleanly leaves them
520	        unapproved rather than failing them at the guard.
521	        """
522	        work = self._work
523	        outcome = work.collateral.resolve(plan.diffs, outcome)
524	        work.derived.build(plan.diffs, outcome.decisions, conflicts=self._conflicts, withheld_esm=self._esm.withheld)
525	        approved_group = any(
526	            diff.item_class in REPO_GROUP_CLASSES
527	            and diff.item_id != METADATA_REFRESH_ITEM_ID
528	            and outcome.decisions.get(diff.item_id) == Decision.APPLY
529	            for diff in plan.diffs
530	        )
531	        if approved_group or work.derived.all_writes() or work.keyrings.pending_work():
532	            marker = metadata_refresh_diff()
533	            # Repo-group items sort before the metadata refresh, packages after it, and
534	            # holds LAST (#208, D8: install-before-hold). Holds are neither package nor
535	            # repo-group, so they are pulled out explicitly rather than folding into the
536	            # pre-marker `non_package` bucket, which would converge them before installs.
537	            repo_like = [
538	                diff for diff in plan.diffs if diff.item_class not in (ItemClass.APT_PACKAGE, ItemClass.APT_HOLD)
539	            ]
540	            package = [diff for diff in plan.diffs if diff.item_class == ItemClass.APT_PACKAGE]
541	            holds = [diff for diff in plan.diffs if diff.item_class == ItemClass.APT_HOLD]
542	            plan = PackagePlan(manager=plan.manager, diffs=(*repo_like, marker, *package, *holds), groups=plan.groups)
543	            outcome = ReviewOutcome(
544	                decisions={**outcome.decisions, marker.item_id: Decision.APPLY},
545	                was_interactive=outcome.was_interactive,
546	                # Carried through verbatim — rebuilding `decisions` above must not drop
547	                # this run's authored snippets/unresolved items.
548	                snippets=outcome.snippets,
549	                unresolved=outcome.unresolved,
550	            )
551	        super().accept_review(plan, outcome)

556	
557	        The interactive flow already cannot produce a `SKIP_ALWAYS` for one — their groups
558	        are absent from `_PROMOTABLE_ACTIONS`, so the promotion screen never offers them —
559	        but "no registry entry" is a property of the model, not of one prompt's wiring, and
560	        a decision can also arrive from the review's automation hook or from a caller

577	    @override
578	    async def apply(self) -> None:
579	        """The base converge loop, preceded under dry-run by the derived `/etc/apt` writes.
580	
581	        A derived write is not a diff, so the base loop has nothing to say about it, and
582	        ADR-014 makes the preview the whole report of a rehearsal: without this, a run whose
583	        entire `/etc/apt` work is derived would preview an `apt-get update` and no reason
584	        for it. On a real run the same facts are logged by the repository unit as each file
585	        lands, which is the honest place for them — the write may still fail.
586	        """
587	        if self.context.dry_run:
588	            for dest in self._work.derived.all_writes():

592	    @override
593	    async def converge(self, diff: ItemDiff) -> CommandResult:
594	        """Route one approved diff to whatever converges it.
595	
596	        Hold items (`apt:hold:<name>`) are routed FIRST, by item_id prefix, so an
597	        `apt:hold:` INSTALL runs `apt-mark hold` rather than falling into the action-based
598	        `apt-get install` dispatch (#208, D4). Repository-group items (pins, apt config,
599	        sources) and the synthetic metadata-refresh marker converge as one ordered,
600	        transactional unit instead — the unit that also provisions and collects signing keys
601	        around its own writes. Unreproducible items are not apt's concern (D-18) —
602	        `manual_installs_sync` owns their snippet replay — so this only ever sees hold,
603	        repository-group, `INSTALL` or `REMOVE` diffs.
604	        """
605	        assert self._accepted_plan is not None
606	        assert self._accepted_outcome is not None
607	        diffs = self._accepted_plan.diffs
608	        decisions = self._accepted_outcome.decisions
609	        work = self._work
610	
611	        if diff.item_id.startswith(APT_HOLD_ID_PREFIX):
612	            return await work.packages.hold(diff)
613	        if diff.item_class in REPO_GROUP_CLASSES or diff.item_id == METADATA_REFRESH_ITEM_ID:
614	            return await work.etc_apt.converge_item(diff, diffs, decisions)
615	        if diff.action == DiffAction.INSTALL:
616	            return await work.packages.install(diff, diffs, decisions)
617	        if diff.action == DiffAction.REMOVE:
618	            return await work.packages.remove(diff, diffs, decisions)
619	        raise ConvergeItemFailed(
620	            f"AptSyncJob.converge: unsupported action {diff.action.value!r} for {diff.label} "
621	            "(only 'install' and 'remove' exist for apt packages)"
622	        )

626	    @override
627	    async def validate(self) -> list[ValidationError]:
628	        """apt-mark availability on both ends, sudo on both ends, dpkg lock free on target.
629	
630	        Sequential checks appending to `errors`, never raising mid-validate (matches
631	        `folder_sync.validate()`'s shape).
632	        """
633	        errors: list[ValidationError] = []
634	
635	        source_check = await self.source.run_command("apt-mark --version")
636	        if not source_check.success:
637	            errors.append(self._validation_error(Host.SOURCE, "apt-mark is not available on source"))
638	
639	        target_check = await self.target.run_command("apt-mark --version", login_shell=False)
640	        if not target_check.success:
641	            errors.append(self._validation_error(Host.TARGET, "apt-mark is not available on target"))
642	
643	        # Source-side sudo matters even though the source is never mutated: capturing
644	        # /etc/apt config runs `sudo find` there, and without passwordless sudo that
645	        # capture degrades to empty digest maps rather than failing. The sync would then
646	        # report success having replicated no repository configuration at all — a silent
647	        # wrong-result, which is worse than refusing to start.
648	        source_sudo_check = await self.source.run_command("sudo --non-interactive true")
649	        if not source_sudo_check.success:
650	            errors.append(
651	                self._validation_error(
652	                    Host.SOURCE,
653	                    "passwordless sudo is not available on source "
654	                    "(required to read /etc/apt repository, keyring and pin config).\n"
655	                    + passwordless_sudo_hint(SOURCE_SUDO_COMMANDS),
656	                )
657	            )
658	
659	        sudo_check = await self.target.run_command("sudo --non-interactive true", login_shell=False)
660	        if not sudo_check.success:
661	            errors.append(
662	                self._validation_error(
663	                    Host.TARGET,
664	                    "passwordless sudo is not available on target "
665	                    "(required to install packages and write /etc/apt config).\n"
666	                    + passwordless_sudo_hint(TARGET_SUDO_COMMANDS, user=self.context.target_username),
667	                )
668	            )
669	
670	        # fuser exits 0 when the file IS held by at least one process, non-zero when
671	        # free (man fuser EXIT CODES) — read-only probe, no lock is acquired or released.
672	        lock_check = await self.target.run_command("sudo fuser /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend", login_shell=False)
673	        if lock_check.success:
674	            errors.append(
675	                self._validation_error(
676	                    Host.TARGET,
677	                    "dpkg frontend lock is held on target (likely unattended-upgrades); "
678	                    "retry once it finishes (RESEARCH Pitfall 5)",
679	                )
680	            )
681	
682	        return errors

6	user installed by hand on the TARGET is something they chose to have, so it becomes its own
7	three-way review item — go ahead, keep the package, or stop the sync.

40	class CollateralEffect(NamedTuple):
41	    """One package the pending transaction would take out from under the user, and the three
42	    ways the review has to say so: the verb for the decision column, the phrase that goes
